--- title: "Principal component analysis" description: "Principal component analysis turns twenty-four taxon columns into a map of the stations. Loadings and scores, how much of the variance the first components hold, and why depth and seabed run diagonally across the map rather than along its axes." order: 4 categories: [unsupervised] --- ## PCA turns 24 taxon columns into one map Twenty-four taxon columns cannot be drawn in one picture. Pairs of them make 276 scatter plots, and none shows the whole community. **Principal component analysis** (PCA) builds new axes from the old columns so that the first two hold as much of the spread as two axes can. Plotted on those two, the stations form a map on which similar communities sit close together. Ecologists call such a map an **ordination**, and PCA is the most widely used way to make one. This page builds the map for the community matrix, shows how to read its axes from their **loadings**, and checks the axes against the recorded depth and seabed. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea PCA finds the direction through the data along which the points spread out most. That direction is the first **principal component**, PC1. The second, PC2, is the direction of most remaining spread at right angles to the first, and so on: there are as many components as columns, ordered by how much of the variance each holds. Keeping the first two or three keeps as much of the spread as two or three numbers can. ::: {.diagram} ![PCA finds the direction of most spread through the data (PC1) and the next at right angles to it (PC2), then reads each point's position along the new axes. Loadings are the weights that build a component from the columns; a score is a point's value on a component; components are ordered by the share of the variance they hold.](img/principal-components.svg){fig-alt="Two cards joined by an arrow, with a strip of definitions below. 1 Find the directions: a cloud of grey points on column A against column B stretches diagonally up to the right; an orange arrow labelled PC1 runs along the longest spread and a shorter blue arrow labelled PC2 at right angles to it. One point is drawn in black. 2 Read the points on them: the same cloud turned so that PC1 runs left to right and PC2 upwards; a dashed line drops from the black point to the PC1 axis, labelled its score on PC1. The strip below reads: loadings, the weights that build a component from the columns, for example PC1 = 0.8 × A + 0.6 × B; score, a point's value on a component, where it sits along that new axis; variance, components are ordered by the share of the spread they hold, PC1 the most."} ::: Each component is a weighted sum of the original columns. The weights are its **loadings**, one per column, and they say what the component is made of. A station's value on a component is its **score**: its position along that axis of the map. Two details matter when reading the results. The columns are put on a common scale first, for the reason [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) gave: otherwise the column with the largest numbers takes over the first component. And a component's **sign is arbitrary**. Flipping every loading and every score gives the same axis pointing the other way, so "high on PC1" means nothing until the loadings say which end is which. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With the columns of $X$ centred and scaled, take the eigen-decomposition of their correlation matrix $S = X^\top X / (n-1)$: $$S v_j = \lambda_j v_j , \qquad \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_p$$ The eigenvector $v_j$ holds the loadings of component $j$, the score of station $i$ is $x_i^\top v_j$, and the eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ is the variance of that component. The share of the variance it holds is $\lambda_j / \sum_k \lambda_k$. ::: ## Worked example ### The first two components hold under a third of the variance The community matrix gets the log and common scale of [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd), and then `step_pca()`, which adds the components to the recipe. `num_comp = 2` keeps the first two as columns for the map; the recipe still records the variance of all 24, and `tidy()` reads it back. scikit-learn's `PCA` does the same job at the end of a pipeline. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) pca_recipe <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = 2) pca_prep <- prep(pca_recipe) # Step 3 of the recipe is the PCA. variance <- tidy(pca_prep, number = 3, type = "variance") |> filter(terms %in% c("percent variance", "cumulative percent variance")) |> pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |> dplyr::select(-id) variance |> slice_head(n = 6) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| component| percent variance| cumulative percent variance| |---------:|----------------:|---------------------------:| | 1| 15.9| 15.9| | 2| 13.5| 29.4| | 3| 6.2| 35.5| | 4| 4.9| 40.4| | 5| 4.5| 44.9| | 6| 4.4| 49.3|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") pca_pipeline = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ("pca", PCA()), ]).fit(taxa_only) pca = pca_pipeline["pca"] variance = pd.DataFrame({ "component": np.arange(1, pca.n_components_ + 1), "percent variance": 100 * pca.explained_variance_ratio_, }) variance["cumulative percent variance"] = variance["percent variance"].cumsum() variance.head(6).round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | component | percent variance | cumulative percent variance | |------------:|-------------------:|------------------------------:| | 1 | 15.9 | 15.9 | | 2 | 13.5 | 29.4 | | 3 | 6.2 | 35.5 | | 4 | 4.9 | 40.4 | | 5 | 4.5 | 44.9 | | 6 | 4.4 | 49.3 | ::: ::: ::: PC1 holds 15.9% of the variance and PC2 13.5%, so the map shows 29.4% of it. From PC3 on, each component holds between 6.2% and 1.8%. A share that low is usual for counts of species. Two stations of the same kind rarely give the same counts: chance alone makes counts vary, and that variation is spread across all 24 columns, so no one direction can hold much of it. The share of the variance tells you how much of the total spread the map shows, not whether what it shows is real. [How many components to keep](dimensionality-reduction.qmd) asks which components carry structure; this page reads the first two. ### Loadings place each taxon by depth and seabed `tidy(type = "coef")` returns the loadings; in scikit-learn they are the rows of `components_`. The table shows the five taxa with the largest loadings on PC1, either sign. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} loadings <- tidy(pca_prep, number = 3, type = "coef") |> filter(component %in% c("PC1", "PC2")) |> pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |> dplyr::select(taxon = terms, PC1, PC2) loadings |> slice_max(abs(PC1), n = 5) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|taxon | PC1| PC2| |:-----|------:|-----:| |tax14 | -0.347| 0.157| |tax13 | -0.340| 0.080| |tax03 | 0.324| 0.194| |tax01 | 0.300| 0.122| |tax02 | 0.297| 0.128|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} loadings = pd.DataFrame(pca.components_[:2].T, columns=["PC1", "PC2"]) loadings.insert(0, "taxon", taxa_only.columns) (loadings.loc[loadings["PC1"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index] .head(5) .round(3) .reset_index(drop=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | taxon | PC1 | PC2 | |:--------|-------:|-------:| | tax14 | 0.347 | -0.157 | | tax13 | 0.34 | -0.08 | | tax03 | -0.324 | -0.194 | | tax01 | -0.3 | -0.122 | | tax02 | -0.297 | -0.128 | ::: ::: ::: The two tabs give the same loadings with **opposite signs**, on both components. Both are correct: R and scikit-learn settle the arbitrary sign by different conventions. The rest of this page reads R's signs; on scikit-learn's, the map is turned upside down and left to right. A table of 48 loadings is hard to read. The figure puts each taxon at its loadings on PC1 and PC2, and adds two things the PCA never saw, worked out from the survey: the average depth at which the taxon was counted (weighted by its counts), and the share of its counts made on hard bottom. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stations_habitat <- community |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") taxon_habitat <- stations_habitat |> pivot_longer(starts_with("tax"), names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |> summarise(mean_depth = weighted.mean(depth_m, count), hard_share = weighted.mean(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), count), .by = taxon) |> inner_join(loadings, by = "taxon") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(taxon_habitat, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = hard_share)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3) + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = round(mean_depth)), size = 3.1, seed = 1, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_colour_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_percent(), name = "counts on\nhard bottom") + labs(x = "loading on PC1", y = "loading on PC2") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each taxon placed by its loadings on the first two components. Colour is the share of its counts made on hard bottom; the label is the average depth at which it was counted, in metres. Neither was given to the PCA.](principal-component-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-loadings-1.png){#fig-loadings fig-alt='Scatter plot of loading on PC2 against loading on PC1, one point per taxon, labelled with its average depth in metres and coloured by the share of its counts on hard bottom. The taxa lie around a ring. The 6 taxa counted mostly on hard bottom, in yellow, sit together in the upper right. The taxa counted mostly on soft bottom run round the lower and left side, from shallow at the lower right to deep at the upper left. 3 taxa sit at the centre, labelled close to the survey average depth of 90 m.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The taxa lie around a ring, and where each one sits matches its habitat. - The 6 taxa counted mostly on hard bottom sit together in the upper right. No other taxon is there. - The rest run round the lower and left side in order of depth, from 53 m at the bottom to 131 m at the far left. - 3 taxa sit at the centre, with loadings near zero on both components. Their average depths, 90 to 91 m, are close to the survey's 90 m, and 23–25% of their counts were on hard bottom, close to the 24% of stations there. They follow neither depth nor seabed, and PCA gave them almost no weight without being told. So both components mix depth and seabed. A taxon's angle round the ring says which mix of the two it follows, and its distance from the centre says how strongly. ### Depth and seabed run diagonally across the components The scores place the stations on the map. Correlating them with the recorded depth and seabed shows which way each increases across it. Correlation runs from −1 to 1, and taken together the two correlations give a direction on the map: an arrow along PC1 for a variable that correlates with PC1 alone, diagonal for one that correlates with both. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stations <- community |> bind_cols(bake(pca_prep, new_data = NULL)) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(hard_bottom = substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel")) directions <- tibble( variable = c("depth", "hard bottom"), PC1 = c(cor(stations$PC1, stations$depth_m), cor(stations$PC1, stations$hard_bottom)), PC2 = c(cor(stations$PC2, stations$depth_m), cor(stations$PC2, stations$hard_bottom))) |> mutate(angle_from_PC1 = atan2(PC2, PC1) * 180 / pi) directions |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)), angle_from_PC1 = round(angle_from_PC1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|variable | PC1| PC2| angle_from_PC1| |:-----------|-----:|----:|--------------:| |depth | -0.67| 0.53| 141| |hard bottom | 0.70| 0.55| 38|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} scores = pca_pipeline.transform(taxa_only) stations = community.assign(PC1=scores[:, 0], PC2=scores[:, 1]).merge( survey[["station_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id") stations["hard_bottom"] = stations["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"]) directions = pd.DataFrame({ "variable": ["depth", "hard bottom"], "PC1": [stations["PC1"].corr(stations["depth_m"]), stations["PC1"].corr(stations["hard_bottom"].astype(float))], "PC2": [stations["PC2"].corr(stations["depth_m"]), stations["PC2"].corr(stations["hard_bottom"].astype(float))], }) directions["angle_from_PC1"] = np.degrees(np.arctan2(directions["PC2"], directions["PC1"])) directions.round(2).round({"angle_from_PC1": 0}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | variable | PC1 | PC2 | angle_from_PC1 | |:------------|------:|------:|-----------------:| | depth | 0.67 | -0.53 | -39 | | hard bottom | -0.7 | -0.55 | -142 | ::: ::: ::: Depth correlates −0.67 with PC1 and 0.53 with PC2; hard bottom correlates 0.70 and 0.55. Neither belongs to one axis. Depth increases along a direction 39° from the nearest axis, and hard bottom along one 38° from it, where 45° would be exactly halfway between two axes. The two directions are 103° apart, close to a right angle. The variance table explains it. PC1 and PC2 hold almost the same share, 15.9% and 13.5%. When two directions carry nearly equal spread, every direction in the plane they make carries nearly the same spread too, so which one PCA takes as PC1 is close to arbitrary. PCA has found the **plane** in which depth and seabed vary, and on the map both are clear. It has no way to know which two directions in that plane matter to an ecologist. Naming PC1 "the depth axis" because depth correlates with it would be wrong here: a component is a direction of large variance, and nothing makes it line up with one driver. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arrows <- directions |> mutate(x = 5 * PC1 / sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2), y = 5 * PC2 / sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2)) ggplot(stations, aes(PC1, PC2)) + geom_point(aes(colour = depth_m, shape = if_else(hard_bottom, "Hard bottom", "Soft bottom")), size = 1.9, alpha = 0.85) + geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 0.7, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + geom_label(data = arrows, aes(x = 1.18 * x, y = 1.18 * y, label = variable), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4, label.size = 0) + labs(colour = "depth (m)", shape = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 800 stations on the first two components, coloured by depth and shaped by seabed. The arrows point the way depth and hard bottom increase, from their correlations with the two components; neither runs along an axis.](principal-component-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-ordination-1.png){#fig-ordination fig-alt='Scatter plot of PC2 against PC1 for 800 stations. Colour runs from dark purple for shallow stations to yellow for deep ones, a smooth ramp with no edge in it. Hard-bottom stations, drawn as circles, form an arm towards the upper right; soft-bottom stations, drawn as triangles, form an arm running from the bottom up to the left. Two arrows leave the origin: depth points up and to the left, hard bottom up and to the right, each about 39 degrees from the nearest axis.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The map shows the two kinds of structure that the earlier pages met. Hard-bottom stations form an arm of their own that meets the soft-bottom arm only in a narrow band: that is the boundary [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) found. Depth shading runs smoothly along each arm with no edge anywhere: a gradient, which k-means and the tree could only cut at an arbitrary depth. A grouping cannot show that difference; the map shows both at once. ## PCA sees straight-line directions PCA finds directions of variance, and only straight ones. A taxon that peaks at middle depths is captured only roughly, and along a long gradient the stations bend into an arch on the map, which ecologists call the **horseshoe effect**. A single station with extreme counts can also pull a component towards itself, so look for isolated points before reading the axes. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Principal component analysis** builds new axes from the columns, ordered by the variance they hold, each at right angles to the last. The first two make a map of the stations, an **ordination**. - **Loadings** are the weights that build a component; a station's position on it is its **score**. Read a component from its loadings, and only after checking its sign: R and scikit-learn gave opposite signs here. - The first two components held 29.4% of the variance. For counts of species that is usual, and it does not mean the map shows nothing. - **A component is not a gradient.** Depth and hard bottom both ran about 39° from the nearest axis, because PC1 and PC2 held nearly equal variance. PCA finds the plane, not the drivers within it. - On the map, the seabed shows as a **boundary** between two arms and depth as a smooth **gradient**. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Remove `step_normalize()` from the recipe, keeping the log. Which taxa now have the largest loadings on PC1, and what do they have in common? 2. Colour the station map by `season` from the survey instead of by depth. Does season line up with either component?
